extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, scholars, and writers seeking an overview of the science fiction genre
extracted.subtask_description: An overview of the science fiction genre intended to inform writers, students, and critics about defining features, classification (hard vs soft), elements commonly used in stories, subgenres, and community/award structures. Useful for deciding what to include in or how to evaluate a science fiction work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of science fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction is a contested category with multiple definitions; encyclopedias and scholars offer differing formulations (the page cites sources such as the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction and the view that 'it is all in the techne').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that definitions vary historically and across critics: some focus on speculative technology or scientific plausibility, others on thematic concerns or techniques. Writers and evaluators should note that what counts as 'SF' depends on chosen definition and context; check taxonomy used (e.g., 'scientific romance', 'speculative fiction') when classifying or pitching work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard vs soft science fiction (feasibility/subject focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A longstanding subdivision centering on the feasibility of the science: 'hard' SF traditionally concerns physics, astronomy, mathematics, and engineering; 'soft' SF concerns biology, mycology, zoology, and the social sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subject-matter and perceived scientific rigor to place a work: Max Gladstone's pithy criterion is stories 'where the math works'. But be aware of criticisms and alternatives: Michael Swanwick defines hard SF by characters striving to solve problems 'in the right way' (ethical/attitudinal traits rather than only technical detail); Ursula K. Le Guin criticizes excluding social sciences as 'not science'. Pitfall: strongly 'hard' works can date when scientific paradigms shift; consider timelessness vs technical rigor when crafting or evaluating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary merit as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Many critics debate whether works of SF have 'literary value'; some SF works are widely considered 'serious' literature while others remain genre fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary merit by considering factors referenced on the page: historical acceptance by the mainstream, the presence of sustained themes, stylistic quality, and recognition (e.g., inclusion in literary canons). Examples of SF authors treated as literary include Mary Shelley, Kurt Vonnegut, Ray Bradbury, Arthur C. Clarke, Doris Lessing. Be aware authors/writers disagree on labels (e.g., Atwood prefers 'speculative fiction').

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven narrative (criterion for 'novel' as literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ursula K. Le Guin's criterion: 'all novels ... deal with character' — a novel attains literary status by using character to make readers 'see' what the author intends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing literary quality of SF, consider depth and centrality of character: does the work use characters as the primary means to explore themes and to engage the reader? Anti-pattern: stories that prioritize idea/exposition over character development risk being labeled less literary according to this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of message within story (idea-driven vs craft-driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orson Scott Card's view: in SF the message and intellectual significance should be contained within the story itself; therefore some conventional literary devices can be omitted if the narrative delivers the intellectual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether thematic or philosophical ideas are embodied in narrative action, character, and plot rather than appended as authorial commentary. Strength: a story whose ideas are organically contained tends to feel cohesive; risk: over-reliance on ideas without craft can read as a 'gimmick' or didactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common science fiction elements (what to include/expect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists prototypical SF elements that a work may include: future or alternative temporal settings; speculative technologies (brain–computer interfaces, bioengineering, AI/superintelligence, robots, advanced weapons); space travel/other-world settings; fictional biological concepts (aliens, mutants, enhanced humans); undiscovered scientific possibilities (teleportation, time travel, FTL travel/communication); social/political systems (utopian, dystopian, post-apocalyptic, post-scarcity); future history/speculative evolution; paranormal abilities (mind control, telepathy, telekinesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when constructing or categorizing a story: many SF works use one or more elements in combination. Consider how each element supports theme/character rather than serving as mere spectacle. Also note recurring motifs such as religion/religious fanaticism as a tool for social critique. The presence of one or more elements tends to mark a work as SF under many definitions, but not all elements are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre classification (taxonomic axis for evaluation and positioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction can be subdivided along many overlapping axes; Gary K. Wolfe identifies over 30 subdivisions. Examples in the page include afrofuturism, cyberpunk, biopunk, climate fiction, space opera, military SF, mundance SF, solarpunk, steampunk, social science fiction, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or marketing a work, identify applicable subgenres because subgenre expectations affect reader reception (tone, pacing, tropes). The page stresses overlapping classifications; a single work may sit in multiple subgenres. Use subgenre labels to set expectations for scientific emphasis, political content, stylistic tone, and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and recognition mechanisms (types of prestige indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different awards have different selection mechanisms which affect prestige and perceived merit: fan-voted awards (e.g., Hugo — voted by Worldcon fans), author/community-voted awards (e.g., Nebula — voted by SFWA membership), jury-selected awards (e.g., John W. Campbell Memorial Award, Theodore Sturgeon Memorial Award), and media/film awards (e.g., Saturn Award).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using awards as a metric of quality, account for selection method and constituency: fan awards measure popularity/fandom enthusiasm, author-voted awards reflect peer esteem, juried awards reflect critical/jury judgment. Regional/subgenre awards and reader polls (Locus) serve narrower tastes. Consider award type when citing prestige or using awards to evaluate a work's reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community composition and inclusion tensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The page notes demographic imbalances (e.g., among Tor Books submissions men accounted for 78% and women 22% in 2013) and community controversies (e.g., the 2015 Hugo Awards voting slates) that highlight tensions between expanding diversity and 'traditional'ist reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider community representation and politics when evaluating the ecosystem: author/audience diversity affects which works are published, awarded, and canonized. Controversies (slates, gatekeeping) may skew award/recognition outcomes and shape perceptions of what constitutes 'acceptable' SF. For creators, awareness of community dynamics can inform positioning, outreach, and the reception likely to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre boundary/labeling as an evaluative choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a work is labeled 'science fiction', 'speculative fiction', 'scientific romance', or another label affects how it is read and judged; some authors resist the SF label for literary or marketing reasons (Atwood prefers 'speculative fiction', Lem spurned the SF label).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or evaluating a work, treat genre labels as strategic and interpretive tools rather than purely descriptive facts. Label choice influences reader expectations, critical framing, and award eligibility. Be explicit about the label you adopt and why, and consider how it will shape evaluation criteria (e.g., expectations for scientific rigor vs thematic exploration).
